catalog_citation: Maddieson, Ian, Sinisa Spajic, Bonny Sands & Peter Ladefoged. 1993. Phonetic structures of Dahalo. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 84: 25-65. (scan at escholarship.org/uc/item/8k45g432)

catalog_quote: 5. Suprasegmentals. Dahalo is a language with pitch accent. Tosco (1991) while admitting that “a lot of work remains to be done in this field” has advanced the understanding of Dahalo tonal processes considerably. In our transcriptions we have assigned each syllable a high (H) or a low (L) tone, marking only the high with an acute accent. The most frequent pattern is for a high tone to fall on the first syllable. Cases where there is more than one high tone on a non-compound word are rare, but all-low words are not unusual. The narrow-band spectrograms provided in Figure 4 enable a few of the tonal properties of the language to be noted. Figure 4c shows a LL word /ʔani/ “head” (11), while 4a shows a HL word /p'úʔʔu/ “pierce” (373). These are the only permitted disyllabic patterns. Generally the low tone immediately following a high shows a rather slow decline of pitch over the syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Dahalo (catalog-all-2026-09-12) with an empty rule and no existing statements; Tosco 1991 supplies the type and placement: two-tone pitch accent system, one lexical tone per word on the penult, obligatory final L, default initial H, no word stress described. Compatible with (and more specific than) the Mous 2022 areal view already held by the project that Cushitic 'pitch accent' languages are restricted tone languages rather than stress languages (Mous does not mention Dahalo).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tosco analyses Dahalo as a two-tone (H/L) pitch accent language of the East Cushitic type: each word carries one lexically specified tone, on the penultimate syllable (H or L); all other surface tones follow from five tonal rules -- TR1 tonally unspecified syllables are L; TR2 Initial High: a word-initial syllable is H unless the following syllable is already H; TR3 Tonal Regression: an affix's tone shifts one syllable leftwards across the morpheme boundary; TR4 Final Low: word-final syllables are always L; TR5 HH -> HL (no two consecutive H). Hence bisyllabic nominals surface only as HL or LL (LH, HH excluded), trisyllables only as HLL (penult L, initial H by TR2) or LHL (penult H); four-syllable nominals likewise by TR2+TR1. Tone mostly accompanies grammatical marking, is 'practically never' the sole carrier of a lexical distinction, but alone distinguishes some verbal paradigm forms (e.g. non-past vs imperfective past of 'beat'). He notes Dahalo differs from typical final/penult pitch accent systems in that H tends to fall on the first syllable. No statement is made in terms of 'stress'; the only use of the word is 'sentence stress' (intonation).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such. The Initial High Rule (TR2) puts an H on the word-initial syllable whenever the penult is not H, so words with a lexically L penult surface with initial H (e.g. HLL trisyllables); Tosco treats this as tonal, not as secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Some 'tonally irregular words' (e.g. the word for 'elder'), perhaps originally containing an affix or nominal formative; words of more than four syllables are always polymorphemic (reduplications, compounds) and get their tones by leftward serial application of the rules; a monosyllabic H particle loses its H in isolation (TR4); under 'sentence stress'/suspensive intonation a final syllable can take H despite TR4; the particle-complex marker can carry the H of a following particle that would otherwise be lost in initial position; author stresses that the tonology of particles and sentence intonation remains little studied. Earlier generative treatment: Elderkin 1974 (rules 'Other Tones Low', 'Initial Tone High', 'Tonal Regression').
new_statements.identity_note: Tosco's data come from two months of fieldwork (Jan-Mar 1988) in Lamu town, Mokowe and Mkunumbi (Lamu District, Coast Province, Kenya); principal informant Dawa Hamadi, born in the Mkunumbi area, bilingual in Amu Swahili. He reports that dialect variability between Dahalo groups is said to be minimal and mainly lexical (southern groups more influenced by Pokomo and Elwana), so the description is not tied to a named dialect.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim on the page scan we hold (printed p. 46, sec. 5) of Maddieson et al. 1993. (2) The deciding source is a first-hand instrumental phonetic study by UCLA phoneticians that states outright 'Dahalo is a language with pitch accent', gives culminativity (more than one H per non-compound word 'rare'), permits all-L words, and shows LL vs HL disyllables — so H presence is lexical and no stress rule exists to code; the tonal-OR-pitch accent exit follows directly. (3) The fuller primary, Tosco 1991 (the language's only grammar), is not yet obtained and could not be downloaded (academia.edu/ResearchGate login walls; no archive.org or repository copy), but the WPP authors cite it precisely for 'tonal processes', so nothing suggests it would move the record toward a stress coding; no newer prosodic study exists (ELAR 2025 deposit is undescribed documentation; Mous 2022 on Cushitic tone

sources.note: Codes Dahalo as 'Simple tone system' (the middle value of 13A: no tones / simple / complex) on the authority of Maddieson et al. 1993, Nurse 1986 and Tucker et al. 1977; a secondhand typological coding consistent with the two-level H/L description already listed here (Maddieson's 'simple' = a two-way contrast), not an independent analysis and silent on the pitch accent question.
